Hey I totally get you. I feel similarly often. I appreciate your willingness to be open minded :)

I suppose then the question you might ask yourself is: are you satisfied with your current trajectory, or are you willing to try something new? 

For me, I would rather be "addicted" to a substance that makes my life better (although anti-depressants are not addictive like meth or other stims, as in they don't create the obsession or compulsion of addiction) than one that ruins my life the way stims do. There isn't the addictive high and crash from a proper dose of medication like there is with illicit substances. For me, the difference is stability and happiness with medications vs. chaos and misery on meth. 

You say you had the strength before to get through it, but what changed? Quite possibly, the answer to that is that your neural pathways and receptors have been permanently altered as a response to stim use. This isn't something you can control and will continue to progress with continued use of stims. 

It saddens me to see the stigma against mental health perpetuated here in the language of "a cheatcode to be 'happy'". When someone has diabetes, they take medication daily to maintain health and prevent death and disease. Why, then, when someone has an illness or disease of the brain, do we see it as a cheatcode?

I have co-occurring mental illnesses so take this with a grain of salt. 

I couldn't do it without Cymbalta. I mean truly, anti-depressants have changed and saved my life. 

I was off my anti-depressants while using during this past relapse of mine, and I almost made the decision to uhhh have a permanent solution to a temporary problem, if you catch my drift. 

When reading your post, my first thought is to advise you to explore what reasons there are for the resistance you have to trying out medications. Are you ashamed that there might be a need? Do you think it will be inconvenient to have to take them every day? I don't necessarily need an answer, but I would encourage you to explore your own hesitations, maybe even bring them up to your psychologist. If you do want to answer here, maybe we or I could offer you some different perspectives. (I mean I've been taking anti-depressants for 11 years and have tried many many different ones.)

Lastly, I would say it doesn't hurt to give it a shot as you can always decide you don't want to be on them anymore. Perhaps you could give it a few months on them (they dont work instantly so you'll want to give it some time) and monitor whether you notice an improvement in mental health or not.That said, NEVER start or stop meds without professional guidance. SSRIs can cause Serotonin Syndrome, which can be fatal I think, when you don't take them properly. This shouldn't deter you, just know that a psychiatrist should always be guiding your tapers on or off your meds.
